title: Excursion trains to Chicago and meeting Louis Armstrong in 1929
summary: Playing in the baggage car on excursion trains to Chicago, meeting Louis at Warwick Hall, and band members taken along.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: When did you first meet Louis, speaking about him? The first time I met Louis to know him was in 1929 in Chicago at the Warwick Hall.
What were you doing up there?
Playing, I used to play the executions out here. The first executions I played out here was on the LNN. And the rest of them, it was 1928. The rest I went up Illinois Central.
Where did the LNN go?

Well she passed through Mobile in those places. She went to Chicago. I see. But you went around like? I went around, yeah, to Birmingham and all those places. It was the longest route, the long route.
Oh yeah. How did the people like you in Chicago?
It was all right. It wasn't that very long. It took eight days for the whole trip. But that's where we would play at, we would have to dance there.
At the Warwick Hall. At the Warwick Hall. Where was Louie?

Well, Louie came over and visited. He knew old man Joe Howard at that time. Old man Joe Howard made that first trip with me, playing the bass. And Louie came over to see him. And Percy, he was there too, Percy. Edwin Washington. Oh, it could be an Edwin.
What was Percy playing? Second trumpet. Percy Humphrey. Percy Humphrey.
Second trumpet.
He was a drummer too when he began, come to think of it. Yeah, he told me.
Oh, I never knew him to play drum. He could have been.
What did Percy do up there? He did all right.
People like him? Oh yeah, it was all right.
How big a band did you have at that time? Eight. Eight, huh? Two trumpets? Two trumpets, two saxes.

Two saxes, two trumpets, bass, drum, banjo, and I don't remember the trombone. I know one time we got a trombone player over there called Hemp. He was an old time musician from here and we got him. But he wouldn't carry no piano. Because mostly I was playing with people in the baggage called Going and Coming. While the train was rolling? No, no, when she'd make stops. Like she'd stop Memphis, Jackson, different places where she'd be over for half an hour or so.
That's where we played. With the people that? Dance, yeah. What else would they do? Have fun.
Having a little drink and stuff. Oh yeah, plenty of drinks. Did they gamble or anything?
No. They didn't gamble. Let's see, you know, I'm not going to play a game. I see, you said you had Edmund Washington, huh? That's Big Fat Wash?

Yeah, Big Wash, Henry Hardin, Tanner Sacks, and old man Joe Howard on that first trip. Joe Phillip, one you call Garsoon, he's playing the banjo. And, uh, Bat Mosley. Was on a drum. Did you ever know Guy Kelly? I'm the one who brought Guy Kelly to Chicago. How's that?
Well, uh, he wanted to go and his mother, his people, was in Chicago.

And, uh, I take them with me. In other words, because they'd hate him with me, he just played when he wanted to, he wanted to make those stops. And that's the last I seen him. He died after that. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He went on up there, huh? Yeah.
He went there. He joined, went up there, and joined some band or another up there.
He was a great trumpet man.
